summary:
Project Salus is a health monitoring platform designed to help protect astronauts on long-duration space missions, where distance from Earth makes reactive care too slow.

We developed a web application (FastAPI, PostgreSQL and React) that brings together each astronaut’s physiological data (heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturation, temperature, sleep, fatigue and mood), medical history, medications and pre-flight baselines. Each crew member is compared with their own baseline rather than a population average. Versioned clinical rules generate alerts that the medical team reviews. We also integrated NASA’s DONKI API to track solar flares, coronal mass ejections and solar energetic particle events, linking them to mission timelines and radiation exposure records.

Our approach is predictive: by combining mission profile, crew health and space environment data, Project Salus is designed to learn from every mission and anticipate risks before they become emergencies, giving health professionals time to act. AI supports decisions; it never replaces the medical team.

Project Salus: predict to protect.
details:
Project Salus is a health monitoring platform for astronauts on long-duration missions. It brings together, in one place, each crew member’s physiological data, mental health indicators, medical history, the mission context and space weather events. The goal is to help health professionals spot risks early instead of reacting after a problem appears.

The current prototype includes:

  • Crew and mission management, with role-based access for astronauts, flight surgeons and mission administrators.
  • Health observations for 12 indicators: heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, temperature, level of consciousness, sleep duration and quality, fatigue, mood, attention and blood glucose. They are shown on an interactive 3D body map and in charts over time.
  • Personal baselines: each astronaut’s readings are compared with their own pre-mission reference, not only with population averages.
  • Deterministic, versioned alert rules that classify readings as caution or critical. Alerts have a full lifecycle (active, acknowledged, resolved) with an audit trail, and critical alerts notify the medical team.
  • Pre-flight screening, medications, allergies and nutrition records.
  • A space weather module that imports solar flares, coronal mass ejections and solar energetic particle events from NASA’s DONKI API, links them into cause-and-effect chains, and relates them to mission timelines. It also includes data models for crew activity (inside the spacecraft, spacewalk or storm shelter), radiation dose records, exposure limits and a 48-hour follow-up after solar particle events, based on NASA’s Human Research Program evidence.
  • A prototype AI assistant that turns free-text symptom reports into structured assessments, grounded in a curated knowledge base of NASA sources.

Benefits

  • Physical, mental, environmental and space weather data in a single view, instead of separate systems.
  • Alerts tailored to each astronaut through personal baselines.
  • Transparent, versioned rules: every alert can be traced to the rule and data that triggered it.
  • Clinical decisions stay with health professionals. The system supports them and never diagnoses.

Intended impact

As missions go farther from Earth, communication delays grow and ground support becomes more limited. Project Salus aims to move astronaut health care from reactive to preventive. The next step is a predictive layer that combines mission profile (destination, duration, phase), crew health trends and space environment data to anticipate risk periods and alert professionals in advance. The system is designed to learn from every mission, so its alerts become more accurate over time and more risks can be prevented.

Tools and technologies

  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, SQLModel, Alembic and PostgreSQL.
  • Frontend: React 19, Vite, TypeScript, Recharts for charts, Three.js for the 3D body map, and Lucide icons.
  • Infrastructure: Docker Compose.
  • Testing: pytest and Playwright.
  • Scientific basis: NASA Human Research Program materials, including Human Health and Performance Risks of Space Exploration Missions (NASA SP-2009-3405).
  • AI: an OpenAI-compatible model provider for the assessment prototype. Claude (Anthropic) assisted with development, research and video production.
  • Hardware: It runs on any computer with Docker and Ollama (or any other local AI).

Creativity

Most health dashboards show vital signs in isolation. Project Salus treats the astronaut’s health in context. For example, a solar flare is shown as a precursor and a solar particle event as an exposure risk, following NASA’s own classification. A spacewalk during such an event raises the level of attention. Our goal is to bring the same idea behind recommendation algorithms (learning from past patterns to anticipate what comes next) to astronaut health. Instead of recommending content, the system recommends attention.

Factors our team considered

  • Scientific grounding: features were mapped to risks documented by NASA’s Human Research Program.
  • Safety and responsibility: the system does not diagnose, rules are explainable, and the medical team makes every decision.
  • Privacy: role-based access and audit logs for every action on health data.
  • Real-world constraints: limited communication far from Earth, a small number of past missions, and the need to compare each person with their own baseline.
  • Honesty about data: the prototype uses fictitious demonstration data, clearly labeled, and keeps simulated data separate from real data.
  • Licensing: we chose free, validated instruments and avoided licensed questionnaires.
